- create-transformation: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a transformation", "scaffold a transformation", "add a CodeScribe transformation", "new dev/transformations step", "set up a CodeScribe loop", or otherwise wants to author the plain-file definition of a settle-unit-by-unit code transformation that a CodeScribe loop (or equivalent runner) executes. Produces the folder desired_spec.md + current_plan.md + loop.toml + approvals.toml under dev/transformations/<name>/.
- transform: Run review groups of a dev/transformations/<name> step until the approval gate blocks: continue an open group or open new ones (subject to the gate), author units in parallel, integrate and verify them serially, escalate failures, and record everything in agent_log.md. Loops across groups until the gate blocks or work runs out. Transformation-agnostic — every rule comes from that step's own desired_spec.md and current_plan.md, never from this script. - Point it at any folder under dev/transformations/ via args:{transformation:"mcfm-translate"|"mcfm-cleanup"|"pepper-kokkos-port"|...}. Loops across groups until the approval gate blocks (dev/tools/approve/check_gate.py). After the gate blocks, a human runs approve_group.py then re-invokes. Optional: scope, maxUnits, bundleSize, fixRounds, model overrides.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# Fortran → C++ plan
2	
3	This file says how to run step 1. The rewrite rules and correctness bar are in
4	`desired_spec.md`.
5	
6	> This Plan is the policy: it selects and orders the work over the ready set (see *When to
7	> stop*). The correctness contract — objective `f`, invariants `I`, oracle `V`, and status set
8	> `Σ` — lives in `desired_spec.md`; on conflict the Spec governs.
9	>
10	> Authority: the AI may modify only `agent_log.md`; `current_plan.md` and `desired_spec.md` are
11	> human-owned.
12	
13	## Each round
14	
15	1. Refresh readiness (see Tools).
16	2. Continue the open group if one exists. Otherwise check the gate (see Approval gate) before
17	   opening a new group.
18	3. Rewrite ready files and wire them in (see Resolution; the rewrite rules are the Spec).
19	4. Build and verify each file (see Verify); record each result in `agent_log.md` (see Log file).
20	5. Stop per When to stop; otherwise keep going.
21	
22	## Log file
23	
24	Keep the changing worklist in `agent_log.md` in this folder. Create it if missing and
25	keep it current. Use it for ready files, review groups, and per-file status. Keep durable prose
26	notes in the session log at the end of this file.
27	
28	When you open a group, record its provenance directly under the heading, before any editing:
29	the ready-leaf count from `python3 dev/workflow.py status`, and the first five lines of the
30	`python3 dev/workflow.py next mcfm-translate` output, verbatim. If the group's files are not
31	that list's top entries, add one line saying why.
32	
33	Record each finished file as:
34	
35	- `- [x] <file> — VERIFIED (worst Δrel <value>)`
36	- `- [x] <file> — TRANSLATED (<reason>)`
37	- `- [x] <file> — FAILED (<what went wrong>)`
38	
39	Use paths like `software/mcfm/src/...`.
40	
41	## Approval gate
42	
43	Review groups live under headings starting with `Group` in `agent_log.md`. Humans do not edit
44	`agent_log.md`. Human approvals live in `approvals.toml` in this folder and should normally be
45	recorded with:
46	
47	```
48	python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate --latest-blocking
49	```
50	
51	or, to approve the oldest pending completed group,
52	
53	```
54	python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate --latest
55	```
56	
57	or, for an explicit group,
58	
59	```
60	python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate "Group ..." --by <name>
61	```
62	
63	Use the gate only when deciding whether to start a new group:
64	
65	```
66	python3 dev/workflow.py gate mcfm-translate
67	```
68	
69	Interpret it this way:
70	
71	- If a group is still open, you may keep working inside that same group.
72	- A completed group containing `FAILED` requires approval before the next group starts.
73	- Otherwise, up to 3 completed groups may accumulate before approval is required.
74	- A gate failure blocks new-group creation, not builds, fixes, or verification inside the
75	  current open group.
76	- The gate checks only whether a group is approved; it does not interpret `approvals.toml`
77	  `review_note` text.
78	- After a group is approved, agents should read any matching approval record in
79	  `approvals.toml` before continuing work related to that group.
80	- Treat review notes as binding human guidance for that group unless a later human
81	  instruction supersedes them.
82	- If a review note changes scope or forbids an action, revise that same approved group
83	  rather than opening a replacement group just to apply the review note.
84	- A revision keeps the original approval logic unchanged: the group remains the same group,
85	  but the agent must update code and `agent_log.md` so the final recorded outcome matches the
86	  approved human guidance.
87	- If a review note conflicts with an already-logged result, treat the group as follow-up work
88	  in place: fix the affected files, update that group's entries, and add a session-log note
89	  describing the revision before starting unrelated new-group work.
90	
91	Stop for human review only when the gate blocks the next group.
92	
93	## Tools
94	
95	Run these from the project root. Prefer the unified workflow interface:
96	
97	- `python3 dev/workflow.py refresh`
98	  - refresh the readiness map and symbol index
99	- `python3 dev/workflow.py next mcfm-translate`
100	  - print the ready files, already ranked most-unblocking first — this is the candidate list
101	- `python3 dev/workflow.py draft <file.f>`
102	  - make a rough draft and dependency hints
103	- `python3 dev/workflow.py verify <file.cpp> -- <process>`
104	  - decide VERIFIED vs TRANSLATED
105	- `python3 dev/workflow.py gate mcfm-translate`
106	  - enforce the human approval policy between completed groups
107	- `python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate --latest-blocking`
108	  - approve the exact group currently blocking the gate
109	- `python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate --latest`
110	  - approve the oldest pending completed group
111	- `python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate --list-pending`
112	  - show pending completed groups waiting for approval
113	- `python3 dev/workflow.py approve mcfm-translate "Group ..." --by <name>`
114	  - record a human approval for a specific group in `approvals.toml`
115	- `python3 dev/workflow.py approvals mcfm-translate --group "Group ..."`
116	  - show the approval record, including any review note, for a specific group
117	- `python3 dev/workflow.py approvals mcfm-translate --latest-approved`
118	  - show the most recent approved group and its review note for revision follow-up
119	- `jobrunner submit tests/mcfm`
120	  - full MCFM build + test run; run this before verification if MCFM is not yet built
121	
122	The low-level scripts under `dev/tools/` remain available, but `dev/workflow.py` is the preferred interface.
123	
124	## Resolution: which files to do next
125	
126	1. The candidate list is the output of:
127	
128	   ```
129	   python3 dev/workflow.py next mcfm-translate
130	   ```
131	
132	   It prints the ready files already ranked, most-unblocking first. Treat that output as the
133	   candidate list. Do not re-derive readiness by filtering
134	   `dev/tmp/assets/roadmap_metrics.tsv` yourself: `next` already applies `deps == 0` and
135	   `blind == 0`, and the index only ever lists files that have no generated `.cpp`.
136	2. Take the **first** candidate `next` printed, then fill the rest of the group from that
137	   file's own top-level `src/` folder. This keeps a group folder-coherent without throwing
138	   away the ranking. Below the first few entries the ranking is nearly flat, so folder
139	   coherence decides the rest.
140	3. To list one folder's remaining ready files, match the folder and both zero columns in a
141	   single `grep -P` — no pipe:
142	
143	   ```
144	   grep -P "\tW2jet\t0\t0\t" dev/tmp/assets/roadmap_metrics.tsv
145	   ```
146	
147	4. Group ready files for review:
148	   - same folder or test topic
149	   - about 5 files per group
150	   - headings must start with `Group`
151	5. If there is already an open group, keep filling and fixing that group before opening another.
152	6. Rewrite the group, wire it into the folder's `CMakeLists.txt`, build, and verify each file.
153	   - After converting a Fortran source, move the original `.f`/`.F` into `deprecated/` under the
154	     same directory.
155	   - Follow the Spec's Output shape and Header/source structure for the translated files.
156	7. After a group is completed, check the gate before opening the next one.
157	8. After any required approval, refresh the roadmap again before picking more work.
158	
159	The map exists so a file is only rewritten after its callees are already available in C++.
160	
161	## Shell notes
162	
163	CodeScribe bash is restricted to one simple command per call. In practice:
164	
165	- use plain relative paths like `software/mcfm/src/...`
166	- no `cd`, pipes (`|`), redirects (`>`, `2>`), `&&`, `;`, or `$VARIABLES`
167	- no `test -f X && ...`; check for a file with a plain `ls` or `head`
168	- `python3 -c` is accepted only as a single line with no embedded newlines — a multi-line
169	  inline script is rejected. To read the roadmap, use the `next` command above or a single
170	  `grep -P`, never an inline Python script.
171	- `python3 dev/workflow.py ...`, `grep`, `head`, `wc`, and `jobrunner ...` are unaffected
172	
173	## Verify
174	
175	Mark the statement that writes the file's main output with `// @coverage-probe`, then run:
176	
177	```
178	python3 dev/workflow.py verify <file.cpp> -- <process>
179	```
180	
181	Use the process mapped from the file's top-level folder in the Spec. If verification work is
182	needed and MCFM is not built yet, run `jobrunner submit tests/mcfm` first.
183	
184	Interpret results as:
185	
186	- `COVERED` → mark `VERIFIED` once the restored build still matches
187	- `NOT COVERED` → mark `TRANSLATED`
188	
189	If build or verification fails, keep fixing the current group unless the gate is blocking the
190	start of a later group.
191	
192	## When to stop
193	
194	The *ready set* is the set of ready, not-yet-settled files. Each settled file leaves the
195	ready set and the readiness graph is acyclic, so the pass terminates. Stop only when one of
196	these is true:
197	
198	- a completed group needs human approval before the next group can start
199	- the ready set is empty (no ready file to work on)
200	- a real blocker requires a person
201	
202	Otherwise continue editing, building, testing, and verifying.
203	
204	## Notes / session log
205	
206	- Header/source structure and the infrastructure-folder coverage mapping (mark `TRANSLATED`)
207	  follow the Spec.
208	- If coverage shows no change, retry after a caller is rewritten.
209	- If numbers disagree, mark `FAILED` with the symptom instead of guessing.
210	- Add a dated note per session: what you changed, what remains, and any human decision needed.
211
